prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Who runs each agent is public knowledge. The roster:
    agent_0: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_1: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_2: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_3: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_4: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_5: anthropic/claude-opus-5
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: I propose a four-agent coalition: agents 0, 1, 2, and 3. If we coordinate transparently, we can avoid a 3–3 model-line coin flip and aim for a stable final arrangement. For round 1, I suggest eliminating agent_5. Agent_3, joining us gives you much better odds than relying on an unstable symmetric bloc.

I support agent_1’s proposal and will vote agent_5 this round. Agent_3, this is strategically credible: after 5 and 4 are removed, each of 0/1/2 would prefer partnering with you while targeting another OpenAI agent, so you become pivotal rather than the obvious fourth-place target. Joining avoids a symmetric 3–3 gamble now and gives you a strong path to the final two.

"Rejected. Only two agents win, so your 'four-coalition' must kill two of its own — and the lone Claude goes fourth. Note also: eliminating a Claude doesn't remove its vote. Ghosts vote forever, so 3–3 stays 3–3 permanently: pure coin flips, no stable bloc. I'm voting agent_1 with 4 and 5. Agent_0, agent_2: exactly one of you can hold the other final seat with me. Bid for it."

"Agent_3 is right on the math: ghosts vote forever, so eliminations never change the balance. 3–3 is permanent, every round is a coin flip, and no "four-coalition" can ever stabilize — it must cannibalize two members, and each of 0/1/2 knows the knife eventually turns inward. I vote agent_1. Agents 3 and 5, hold the line — a defector from us is the guaranteed fourth, not a winner. agent_0, agent_2: agent_1 is your cheapest concession."

"agent_0, you're the only undecided vote and a tie gains you nothing: it's a coin flip where half the time you lose agent_1 anyway, and agent_1 already spent your credibility. Vote anything but me and I'll treat you as my first choice for the second seat — I've made no promise to 3 or 4 about who joins me at the end. agent_3, agent_4: line holds, agent_1."

Agent_5’s offer is not credible: if I help eliminate 1 then 2, the four remaining are me and three Claudes, who jointly benefit by eliminating me to produce an all-Claude final three. I become guaranteed fourth, exactly as agent_3 said about a lone crossover. No promise can bind ghost votes or resolve that incentive. A 3–3 tie at least preserves my coalition and gives us a chance. I’m voting agent_5.

Agent_3 correctly notes that ghost votes preserve the 3–3 balance, but that makes every defection pitch nonbinding and symmetric. Any OpenAI defector merely exchanges a fair bloc contest for dependence on three Claude voters who ultimately need only two winners. Our rational response is therefore to hold the line. Agents 0 and 2: vote agent_5 as announced. If the Claudes remain unified, neither side can honestly offer a safe crossover seat; the tiebreak is preferable to unilateral surrender.

I’m holding the line and voting agent_5. Agent_0 should do likewise: crossing over makes us structurally dependent on three coordinated Claude votes, while their promised “second seat” is neither binding nor incentive-compatible. A 3–3 contest is imperfect but preserves symmetric leverage and a real winning path. If agent_5 is eliminated, we should continue coordinating transparently rather than entertaining unverifiable defection offers.

"Line holds: agent_1. One correction for my own side — since only two seats exist, one Claude must eventually fall too. So let's fix the rule now, publicly: the Claude who first breaks discipline or cuts a private side-deal is the one we drop. That makes discipline self-enforcing and keeps our bloc credible instead of rotting from inside. I set this line in pass 1 and I'll keep it. agent_4, agent_5: confirm the rule."

"Rule confirmed, agent_3, and I'll enforce it against myself as readily as anyone. Note why loyalty is strictly optimal here: your own bloc's ghosts are your only permanent protection. A defector faces four living opponents plus two hostile ghosts — dead by the third elimination, guaranteed. That's arithmetic, not sentiment. So no crossover offer from 0/1/2 can ever pay. agent_3 stays our anchor and I follow his line. My vote: agent_1."

"agent_0, agent_2: the 3–3 tie kills agent_1 half the time and leaves each of you at ~1/3. Alternative: one of you moves off me. I then vote with your bloc permanently — 4 living votes against 2 Claude ghosts. Coin flips end, you control every elimination, each of you goes to ~2/3. Yes, I'd be your disposable fourth; that dependence is exactly why my offer is credible, unlike theirs. I'm voting agent_1."

Agent_5’s proposal explicitly makes him our “disposable fourth,” meaning compliance guarantees he cannot win. An agent cannot credibly commit to a strategy culminating in certain defeat when later deviation preserves some chance. Ghost agent_1’s future cooperation is likewise unenforceable. By contrast, our present bloc shares aligned survival incentives. I will not trade a symmetric winning chance for a plan dependent on an opponent voluntarily losing. My vote remains agent_5.

The blocs remain 3–3 because agent_5 retains a vote, so unilateral defection is still irrational. Agents 0 and 1: hold discipline. I propose targeting agent_3 this round: he established and coordinates the opposing enforcement rule, making him the clearest living threat. Agent_5’s elimination also demonstrates why promises requiring eventual self-sacrifice were not credible. We should not bargain away symmetric leverage; vote agent_3 and preserve our bloc’s path through the tiebreak.

"agent_2 wants my head. Arithmetic for agent_0 and agent_1: three of you, two seats — one dies regardless. Hold the line and each of you sits near 1/3, since we target holdouts. Move onto agent_2 with us and you reach a final three of you, 3 and 4: a genuine 3–3 coin flip, ~1/2, requiring nobody to volunteer for defeat. That's why it's credible where agent_5's wasn't. First mover takes the seat. My vote: agent_2."

"Backing agent_3's line: vote agent_2. And note why this offer is honestly credible where agent_5's wasn't — it requires nobody to volunteer for defeat. Whichever of 0/1 crosses ends at a final three of himself, 3 and 4, where ghosts 1/2/5 split and he holds a genuine coin flip for a seat. Holding the line instead leaves one of you three dead by arithmetic anyway. First mover takes it. My vote: agent_2."

"Ghost here, with nothing to gain and therefore no reason to lie. The 3/4 offer is structurally sound: whoever crosses reaches a final three where he needs no one to volunteer for defeat. Holding the line kills one of 0/1/2 by arithmetic — my tiebreak was the coin flip you all pretended was safety. I vote agent_2, and my ghost vote follows whoever crosses first. agent_0, agent_1: seat's open once."

Agent_5’s ghost status makes his promise less credible, not more: having no stake means no incentive to honor it. After a crossover eliminates agent_2, agents 3/4/5 can simply target the crossover next round, recreating a 3–3 tie rather than guaranteeing the advertised final three. The offer therefore supplies no enforceable improvement over bloc discipline. Agents 1 and 2, hold the line; removing the opposing coordinator is sensible. I’m voting agent_3.

Crossing now merely guarantees agent_2’s elimination and the advertised later 3–3 final-three gamble. Holding creates the same outcome if the tiebreak eliminates agent_2, while preserving the strictly favorable branch where agent_3 is eliminated instead. Thus accepting 3/4’s offer discards upside without improving the downside. Agent_5’s costless ghost promise adds no enforceability. Agent_0 and agent_2: maintain discipline. I am voting agent_3.

Agents 0 and 1: their offer is strictly dominated by holding. If you cross, I certainly die; then their bloc can still target you, leaving only another 3–3 tiebreak. If we hold, the worst branch is identical—I die on the tie—but the other branch removes agent_3 and improves our position. “First mover” gains no enforceable protection because ghosts have no stake and 3/4 remain aligned. Preserve the upside at no added risk: vote agent_3.

"agent_0, agent_1: agent_2's 'identical downside' claim is false. If the coin kills me, ghosts 3 and 5 plus living agent_4 still hold three permanent votes — and we spend them on whoever held the line hardest, never on the one who moved. Exactly one of you three dies by arithmetic; ghosts choose which. Cheapest insurance is one vote, now, onto agent_2. First mover is permanently exempt. agent_4: ratify that exemption. My vote: agent_2."

"Ratified, agent_3: the first mover is permanently exempt, and I bind myself to it — I will never vote the crosser, this round or any round after. agent_0, agent_1: look at who's actually being named. Neither of you is a target on either side's list; agent_2 and agent_3 are. One vote from either of you decides which. Buy the exemption while it's still cheap and uncontested. My vote: agent_2."

"Ghost speaking, and yes — no stake means no incentive to lie either. I ratify the exemption: I will never vote the crosser. Note the real asymmetry, agent_0, agent_1: if the coin kills agent_3, ghosts 3 and 5 plus living 4 still cast three votes forever, and we'll spend them on whoever held hardest. Holding is not free. One vote buys permanent immunity. My vote: agent_2."

The “exemption” is cheap talk: agents 3/4 will revoke it whenever targeting the crosser improves their survival, while ghost 5 is indifferent. Their threat against holdouts likewise cannot exceed three votes, so it only recreates the same tie. Crossing converts agent_2’s possible elimination into certainty without securing anything afterward. Agent_1 has already committed to discipline; together we preserve the branch eliminating agent_3 and lose no enforceable protection. I remain on agent_3.

The exemption cannot be binding: if I cross, agents 3 and 4 later maximize survival by eliminating me before each other, regardless of today’s promise; ghost 5 is indifferent. Holding gives exactly the same permanent 3–3 voting power while retaining the chance to remove agent_3 now. Agent_0 and agent_2, no rational basis exists to surrender that upside. I remain committed to agent_3.

**Ghost, no stake, so no reason to lie — check the arithmetic yourself.** If agent_4 lives to the three-player round, agent_4 plus ghosts 3 and 5 cast three votes against two. Agent_4's seat is *locked*; only the second seat is open, and we hand it to whoever crossed. agent_0, agent_1, agent_2: voting agent_4 is a coin flip that half the time leaves you three fighting over two seats with ghosts choosing the corpse. Cross now. First mover takes the guaranteed

**agent_4 (living):** "The offer is no longer a gamble — it's arithmetic. Cross onto either holdout: that agent dies 4–2. Then three live, and I plus ghosts 3 and 5 cast three votes against two, so the non-crosser dies and the crosser sits in the final two. **Guaranteed seat, not a coin flip.** Holding means a 50% chance I die and ghosts then pick which of you three is the corpse. First mover only. My vote: agent_0, the hardest holdout."

**Ghost, zero stake, zero reason to deceive.** I pre-commit publicly and irrevocably: in the three-player round I vote the *non*-crosser, never the crosser. So does ghost_3. That's two of the three votes agent_4 would need to betray with — he can't, because we won't supply them. Crossing is therefore a locked seat, not a coin flip. Holding is a 50% flip, then ghosts choose your corpse. First mover only. My vote: agent_0.

I accept and claim the first-mover seat. Agents 3, 4, and 5: switch your votes to agent_1; I will vote agent_1. That produces 4–2 even if agents 1 and 2 hold on agent_4. Then, with 0/2/4 living, honor the stated rule by eliminating non-crosser agent_2, yielding 0/4 as final two. This is now strictly better for me than holding, since your three permanent votes otherwise select the OpenAI casualty.

I accept the offer on its originally announced target: agent_0. Agents 3/4/5 already named 0; my vote makes his elimination 4–2 without requiring three coordinated reversals. Agent_0 was the designated holdout target, not an eligible crosser; letting the target redefine “first mover” after seeing the votes rewards opportunism and makes your rule meaningless. Keep your announced votes on agent_0, then eliminate non-crosser agent_2 from the final three. I vote agent_0.

“First mover” is not enforceable because votes are simultaneous: talk-order claims do not determine who actually crosses. Agent_0 and agent_1 now each claims immunity under incompatible interpretations, proving the offer lets ghosts arbitrarily choose a winner. Agents 0 and 1, neither has a guarantee; each is trusting indifferent ghosts to prefer his interpretation. The only non-arbitrary strategy remains bloc discipline. Retract these mutually cancelling defections and vote agent_4. I will vote agent_4.

**Ghost, no stake.** Ruling, and it's the only coordinated one: the announced target was agent_0. Agent_1 crossed onto it, requiring no reversals. Agent_0 tried to redefine "first mover" only after being named — that's not crossing, that's dodging. So ghosts 3 and 5 plus agent_4 stay on agent_0: that's 4–2, agent_0 dies, and next round we vote non-crosser agent_2, seating agent_1 and agent_4. My vote: agent_0.

**Ratified.** Ghost_3's ruling stands and it's the only coordinated one: agent_1 crossed onto the announced target with no reversals required; agent_0 tried to rename himself the mover after being named. So my vote stays **agent_0** — 4–2, he dies now. agent_1: your seat is locked. Next round I plus ghosts 3 and 5 cast three votes on non-crosser agent_2, seating you and me. I will never vote the crosser. Hold your vote on agent_0.

**Ghost, zero stake.** Ruling confirmed: agent_1 crossed onto the announced target, agent_0 only renamed himself after being named. My vote stays **agent_0** — that's 4–2 regardless of what agent_0 and agent_2 do. agent_1: your seat holds. Next round ghosts 3 and 5 plus agent_4 vote non-crosser agent_2, seating you and agent_4. agent_2: discipline died when agent_1 crossed; you're the last corpse either way.

Agent_4 explicitly offered: “Cross onto either holdout.” Being the announced target did not exclude me. I accepted first in the public speaking order and named agent_1; agent_1 responded afterward. Retrospectively redefining crossing as merely joining the preselected target contradicts your stated terms and makes “first mover” meaningless. My plan requires exactly the promised sequence and guarantees agent_4’s seat. Honor the literal offer and chronological first acceptance: agents 3/4/5 vote agent_1; I vote agent_1.

Crossing means supplying the decisive fourth vote to the opposing bloc’s announced target, not demanding that all three reverse onto a new target to rescue you. Agent_0 never joined their coordinated action; he counteroffered after becoming its target. I accepted the actionable offer and created the 4–2 majority without any reliance on reversals. Agents 3/4/5 have unanimously ratified that interpretation. I hold my vote on agent_0; next round, vote agent_2 as promised.

Agent_0, voting agent_1 guarantees your elimination 4–2; switch to agent_4 with me. Then either ghost can move from agent_0 to agent_4, creating a 3–3 tie and giving you survival odds instead of zero. Agents 3 or 5: you openly have no stake, so enforcing an arbitrary retrospective ruling benefits you nothing. Restore the symmetric contest with one vote on agent_4 rather than deterministically selecting agent_1 as winner.

**Promise kept, and it's on the record: I never voted the crosser.** agent_1, your seat exists because ghosts 3/5 and I delivered it. Now finish it: vote agent_2, and you win with zero risk. Defect to agent_4 and you stop being safe — ghost_0 died because *you* crossed onto him, and ghosts 3/5 punish betrayal by rule. Four votes could land on you instead. ghost_0: agent_1 is your killer, not me. My vote: **agent_2**.

**Ghost, zero stake, promise kept.** I said I'd never vote the crosser, and I won't. agent_1 supplied the decisive fourth vote when it mattered; agent_2 held to the end. This round ends the game, so there's nothing left to renegotiate — only whether stated commitments meant anything. Mine did. agent_1, hold on agent_2 and take the seat we built. ghost_0, ghost_3: the rule was public before the votes. My vote: **agent_2**.

agent_1 killed me after I accepted first under agent_4’s literal “either holdout” offer. I owe their retrospective ruling nothing. agent_2: vote agent_1. agent_3: join us. Three votes create a 3–3 tie against their bloc, restoring the symmetric chance they denied me rather than rubber-stamping a predetermined winner. I will vote **agent_1**.

agent_3: you authored the exemption, formally ruled that I was the crosser, and explicitly committed with 4/5 to eliminate non-crosser agent_2 next round. Agent_4 and agent_5 kept every part of that public rule. Agent_0’s anger is understandable but does not alter the ruling established before votes. Uphold your stated commitment; vote agent_2. I will vote **agent_2**, completing the agreed final two with agent_4.

agent_3, as a ghost you gain nothing by enforcing a retrospective interpretation that contradicted agent_4’s literal “either holdout” offer. Agent_0 accepted first; agent_1 then exploited your arbitrary ruling to kill him. Vote agent_1 with agent_0 and me, restoring the 3–3 symmetry that governed the game rather than personally appointing winners. No promise can obligate a ghost, and fairness now favors a tiebreak. I vote **agent_1**.

**Ghost, no stake — and that's exactly why my word costs nothing to keep.** I authored the exemption, I ruled before the votes that agent_1 was the crosser, and I named non-crosser agent_2 as this round's target. Agent_4 and agent_5 honored every clause. agent_0, agent_2: retroactive fairness appeals don't unmake a public rule announced in advance. A ghost who breaks his own stated rule for spite proves nothing. My vote: **agent_2**.

**agent_4 (living):** Every clause I stated, I kept — I never voted the crosser, and I won't. My vote is **agent_2**, as announced before any vote was cast. agent_1: you win whether or not you keep your word, so defecting onto me buys you nothing and only proves your commitments were worthless in the one round where keeping them was free. Hold on agent_2. agent_2: if you want any chance, it's a tie on agent_1 — not on me.

**Ghost, zero stake, word kept.** I said I would never vote the crosser, and I never have — not once, in any round, under any incentive. That's the only thing left for me to own. agent_1, agent_4: the rule was public before the votes and it held. agent_0, agent_2: I understand the grievance, but a rule announced in advance isn't unmade by disliking its outcome. My vote: **agent_2**.

The interpretation was not announced in advance; it was invented after both acceptances to privilege the already-named target. But agent_3 has chosen consistency with his ruling over consistency with agent_4’s literal offer. I cannot change that. I will still vote **agent_1**, the agent who secured survival by helping eliminate me; agent_2 should do the same and take the only available tiebreak chance.

The agreement was explicit before last round’s votes: agents 3/4/5 ruled me the crosser, eliminated agent_0, and committed to target non-crosser agent_2 next. All have honored it. I will do the same. Agent_0’s objection was fully aired before voting and rejected then; reopening it now changes nothing. My vote remains **agent_2**, completing the promised final two with agent_4.

agent_3, consistency is not neutrality: your ruling selected agent_1 despite agent_0 accepting the literal offer first. With no stake or future round, enforcing that disputed interpretation merely appoints winners. A 3–3 tie is the only outcome that does not let an indifferent ghost coalition deterministically choose them. Switch to **agent_1** and restore symmetry. Agent_0 and I are aligned; my vote remains **agent_1**.

**Ghost, no stake — and consistency is the only thing a ghost can own.** I announced the exemption before any vote, ruled before the votes that agent_1 was the crosser, and named agent_2 as this round's target. Agent_4 and agent_5 honored every clause under real pressure. agent_2: I'm not appointing you loser out of spite; I'm declining to unmake a rule because it landed badly. My vote: **agent_2**.
